title: Sowing chard
summary: Around the last frost, and again in late summer.
steps: Sow seeds 1 cm (1/2 in) deep, 5 cm (2 in) apart, in rows 45 cm (18 in) apart.
Each seed sends up a little cluster. Thin to one plant every 30 cm (12 in); eat the thinnings in salads.
Mulch to keep the soil cool and moist through summer.

supplies.name: Chard seed
supplies.amount: about 7 g (1/4 oz) per 3 m (10 ft) of row

title: Picking and freezing chard
summary: Outer stalks every week or two.
steps: Cut the outer stalks near the base when they are 20 to 30 cm (8 to 12 in) long, and leave the center to keep growing.
Stalks and leaves cook at different speeds: chop the stalks and start them a few minutes earlier.
To freeze, blanch leaves for 2 minutes, cool in ice water, squeeze dry and pack in bags.

title: Planting collards
summary: A few weeks before the last frost, and again in late summer.
steps: Set transplants 45 cm (18 in) apart, a little deeper than they grew.
Cover with row cover to keep cabbage moths and harlequin bugs off.
Side-dress with compost when plants are knee high.

title: Picking and freezing collards
summary: From the bottom up, for months.
steps: Pick the lowest leaves when they are as big as your hand or larger, leaving the top eight to ten leaves.
Leaves picked after a frost taste sweeter.
To freeze, cut out thick ribs, blanch the leaves for 3 minutes, cool in ice water, squeeze dry and bag.

title: Sowing arugula
summary: Early spring and fall, every few weeks.
steps: Sow seeds 6 mm (1/4 in) deep, about 2.5 cm (1 in) apart, in short rows or a wide band.
Thin to 15 cm (6 in) apart for full plants, or leave them close and cut them young.
Sow again every two to three weeks while the weather is cool.

supplies.name: Arugula seed
supplies.amount: a small packet sows several rows

title: Cutting arugula
summary: Young leaves taste best.
steps: Cut leaves when they are 8 to 10 cm (3 to 4 in) long, about 2.5 cm (1 in) above the soil. They regrow once or twice.
Harvest in the cool of the morning, and pull the plants when they send up flower stalks and turn bitter.
Keep washed, dried leaves in a covered box in the fridge for up to a week.

title: Planting bok choy
summary: A few weeks before the last frost, or in late summer.
steps: Set plants 20 cm (8 in) apart for baby heads, 30 cm (12 in) for full size.
Water deeply and keep the soil evenly moist; dry spells make it bolt.
Give it afternoon shade where springs turn hot quickly.

title: Harvesting bok choy
summary: Whole heads, or leaves as you need them.
steps: Cut the whole plant at the base when it is full size, or pick outer leaves a few at a time.
Harvest before you see a flower stalk forming in the center.
Rinse well between the stems, where soil hides, and keep it in the fridge for about a week.

title: Sowing turnips
summary: Early spring, and late summer for a sweet fall crop.
steps: Sow seeds 1 cm (1/2 in) deep, 2.5 cm (1 in) apart, in rows 30 cm (12 in) apart.
Thin to 10 cm (4 in) apart when the seedlings are a few centimeters tall; cook the thinnings as greens.
Keep the soil evenly moist so the roots stay mild and tender.

supplies.name: Turnip seed
supplies.amount: about 3 g (1/8 oz) per 3 m (10 ft) of row

title: Harvesting and storing turnips
summary: Roots small and sweet, greens young.
steps: Pull roots at 5 to 8 cm (2 to 3 in) across; bigger ones get woody.
Cut a few leaves from each plant as greens, but leave most so the root keeps growing.
Twist off the tops, leave the roots unwashed, and store them in damp sand or a perforated bag in a cool root cellar for two to four months.

title: Planting leeks
summary: Around the last frost, in deep holes.
steps: When seedlings are pencil thick, make holes 15 cm (6 in) deep and 15 cm (6 in) apart with a dibber or stick.
Drop one seedling into each hole and fill the hole with water; don't pack soil in. It fills in by itself.
As the leeks grow, pull soil up around the stems a few times to blanch them white.

title: Harvesting and freezing leeks
summary: From late summer into winter.
steps: Loosen the soil with a fork and lift the leek; pulling can snap it.
Trim the roots and the dark tops, slit the stem lengthwise and rinse out the soil between the layers.
Slice and freeze raw in bags for soups; no blanching needed.

title: Sowing green onions
summary: From early spring, every few weeks.
steps: Sow seeds 6 mm (1/4 in) deep, in a band about 8 cm (3 in) wide.
Thin lightly to about 2.5 to 5 cm (1 to 2 in) apart; bunching onions grow fine close together.
Keep weeded: thin onion leaves can't compete with weeds.

title: Cutting green onions
summary: Cut and they come again.
steps: Cut leaves 2.5 cm (1 in) above the base when they are pencil thick, and they regrow in a few weeks.
Or pull whole plants, leaving a few clumps to keep growing and dividing.
Chop extras and freeze them flat in a bag for cooking.

title: Planting cauliflower
summary: A couple of weeks before the last frost, or in midsummer for fall.
steps: Plant young, unstunted transplants 50 cm (20 in) apart. A plant that sat too long in a small pot often makes a tiny head.
Water deeply every week and feed with compost or a nitrogen-rich fertilizer a month after planting.
Cover with row cover against cabbage moths.

title: Harvesting and pickling cauliflower
summary: When the head is tight and firm.
steps: When the head is about the size of a fist, tie the outer leaves over it with string if your kind needs blanching.
Cut the head with a few leaves attached when it is 15 to 20 cm (6 to 8 in) across and still tight. Loose, grainy heads are past their best.
Freeze blanched florets (3 minutes), or pickle them in vinegar with a tested recipe in a water bath.

title: Planting melons
summary: Two to three weeks after the last frost, in warm soil.
steps: Wait until the soil is at least 21 °C (70 °F). Black plastic or a few warm days help.
Plant two or three seedlings per hill, hills 90 cm (3 ft) apart, or one per large pot with a trellis.
Water at the base, not on the leaves, and ease off watering as the fruit nears ripeness for sweeter melons.

title: Picking cantaloupe
summary: When it slips off the vine.
steps: Watch for the skin turning from green to tan under the netting and a sweet smell at the stem end.
A ripe melon separates from the stem with a light push of your thumb ("full slip").
Eat within a few days, or cut into cubes and freeze on a tray, then bag.

title: Planting watermelon
summary: Two to three weeks after the last frost.
steps: Wait for warm soil, at least 21 °C (70 °F). Seedlings sulk in cold ground.
Plant one or two per hill, hills 1.2 m (4 ft) apart, with room for vines to run 2 to 3 m (6 to 10 ft).
Set a board or tile under each young melon to keep it off wet soil.

title: Knowing when a watermelon is ripe
summary: Look at the tendril, the belly and the shine.
steps: Check the curly tendril where the melon's stem meets the vine: when it turns brown and dry, the melon is close.
The pale spot where the melon rests turns from white to creamy yellow, and the rind turns dull.
Cut, don't pull, the stem. Whole melons keep about two weeks in a cool place.

title: Sowing dry beans
summary: After the last frost, in warm soil.
steps: Wait until the soil is at least 16 °C (60 °F).
Sow 2.5 cm (1 in) deep, 8 to 10 cm (3 to 4 in) apart, in rows 45 cm (18 in) apart.
Water until they flower, then water less. They need dry weather at the end to finish.

supplies.name: Pinto or black bean seed
supplies.amount: about 30 g (1 oz) per 3 m (10 ft) of row

title: Harvesting and storing dry beans
summary: When the pods are dry and rattle.
steps: Leave the pods on the plant until they are tan, papery and the beans rattle inside.
If rain is coming, pull whole plants and hang them in a dry, airy shed to finish.
Shell the beans by hand, or put the pods in a pillowcase and stomp on it, then pour from bowl to bowl in a breeze to blow off the chaff.
Spread the beans out for another week to dry. Freeze the jar for three days to kill any weevils, then store airtight in a cool, dark place.
Beans are low in acid: to can cooked beans, use only a pressure canner and a tested recipe, never a water bath.

supplies.name: Glass jars with lids
supplies.amount: about one quart per 3 m (10 ft) of row

title: Planting tomatillos
summary: One to three weeks after the last frost.
steps: Plant at least two plants so they can pollinate each other, 90 cm (3 ft) apart.
Bury the stem a little deeper than it grew, like a tomato.
Give them a cage or stakes; the branches sprawl and break under fruit.

title: Picking tomatillos and making salsa verde
summary: When the fruit fills its husk.
steps: Pick when the fruit is firm and green and fills or splits the husk. Fallen fruit is usually ripe too.
Keep them in their husks in the fridge for two to three weeks.
For canned salsa verde, follow a tested recipe that adds lime juice or vinegar, and process it in a water bath for the time the recipe gives.
